title: The problem retrieval actually solves
description: Why a corpus too large for context isn't a context-window problem to solve by paying for a bigger window — it's a selection problem that retrieval exists to solve.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a large corpus is a selection problem, not just a context-size problem
Identify when retrieval is the right tool versus when the previous module's context-engineering techniques are enough on their own

contentSections.title: Bigger context isn't the same fix

contentSections.body: A team's support agent needs to answer questions against 4,000 help-center articles, roughly 6 million tokens of text. Someone proposes switching to the largest available context window and pasting the whole knowledge base in. It technically doesn't fit even the largest commercial context window — and if it did, every single question, including "how do I reset my password," would cost millions of tokens to answer.

contentSections.scenario: The previous module covered deciding what's always-present versus fetched on demand for a *known, small* set of things (an endpoint reference, a policy document). This team's corpus is 4,000 articles — orders of magnitude larger, and which article matters depends entirely on a question that hasn't been asked yet.
contentSections.question: What's actually different about this case from last module's fetch-on-demand pattern?

options.label: The problem isn't naming a specific thing to fetch — it's finding *which* few articles, out of thousands, are even relevant to an arbitrary incoming question
Nothing is different — this is the same fetch-on-demand pattern, just with more items to choose from
The only real difference is that this corpus needs a bigger context window to hold it all

feedback.selection: Right. Last module's `lookup_endpoint(name)` pattern works because the model already knows *which* endpoint to ask for — the name is in the question. Here, nothing tells you in advance which of 4,000 articles is relevant; that has to be figured out from the question itself, which is a search problem, not a simple named lookup.
feedback.same: The mechanism is genuinely different, not just bigger — a named lookup tool works because the *name* of what to fetch is known ahead of time. At this scale, the relevant item isn't named anywhere; it has to be found by matching the question's meaning against thousands of candidates, which needs a real search step, not a lookup by name.
feedback.bigger-window: A bigger window doesn't solve the actual problem, which isn't fitting the text — it's finding the *right few articles* out of thousands without paying to consider all of them on every single question, most of which are irrelevant to any given query.

contentSections.concept: **Retrieval** is the step that turns "a large corpus exists somewhere" into "here are the few pieces of it relevant to this specific question" — a search-and-rank problem, not a fetch-by-name problem and not a fit-it-all-in problem. It matters exactly when the relevant subset can't be known in advance and is a small fraction of a corpus too large to include wholesale.

contentSections.body:
The pattern most people call "RAG" (retrieval-augmented generation) is exactly this: retrieve the small relevant slice of a large corpus, then hand only that slice to the model as context for its answer. Mechanically, it's three stages:

```
1. INDEX (done ahead of time, once, and re-run when the corpus changes)
   corpus (4,000 articles) → chunks → embeddings → stored in a searchable index

2. RETRIEVE (done per question, at answer time)
   question → embed the question → search the index → top-k most relevant chunks

3. GENERATE (done per question, using only what was retrieved)
   top-k chunks + question → model generates an answer grounded in those chunks
```

The expensive, offline step (indexing 4,000 articles) happens once, not per question. The cheap, online step (retrieving the top handful of chunks for one specific question) happens every time — and it's cheap precisely because it doesn't require considering all 4,000 articles' full text at answer time, only searching a pre-built index of them.

Retrieval solves a selection problem — finding the small relevant slice of a corpus too large to include wholesale — not a fitting problem a bigger context window would solve, and not a naming problem last module's fetch-by-name pattern would solve.

contentSections.title: When retrieval is the wrong tool, too

contentSections.body: A team building an internal agent has exactly six tools and a 40-line system prompt describing what the company does. Someone suggests "adding RAG" to make the agent "smarter about company context." There's no large corpus here — just a small, fixed, always-relevant amount of information that already fits comfortably in a normal system prompt.

contentSections.scenario: This team's total "company context" is about 2,000 tokens: what the company does, its six tools, and a handful of hard constraints — all of it relevant to essentially every question the agent will ever get.
contentSections.question: Why would adding a retrieval layer here be the wrong move, mechanically?

options.label: Retrieval solves the problem of a corpus too large to include wholesale and not known in advance which piece is relevant — neither is true here, so it adds indexing infrastructure, embedding cost, and retrieval latency to solve a problem that doesn't exist
Retrieval systems are always worse than a plain system prompt, in every case
The company's information is too sensitive to be embedded

feedback.no-problem: Right. Everything about this team's 2,000 tokens is already always-relevant and already fits easily — there's no large corpus to select from and no uncertainty about what's needed. Retrieval infrastructure (an index to build and keep in sync, an embedding step, a search step) is real cost and real latency added to solve a selection problem this case doesn't have.
feedback.always-worse: Too broad — the support-agent case earlier in this lesson genuinely needed retrieval, because 4,000 articles is a real selection problem a system prompt can't solve. The point isn't that retrieval is bad; it's that it solves a specific problem this small, fixed, always-relevant case doesn't have.
feedback.sensitivity: Nothing in the scenario suggests a sensitivity concern — the actual mismatch is scale and relevance-certainty, not what the content is about.

contentSections.mechanism: Retrieval earns its cost (an index, an embedding step, retrieval latency on every question) when a corpus is too large to include wholesale *and* which piece is relevant can't be known ahead of the question. When both of those are false — content is small and always relevant — a retrieval layer adds real infrastructure and latency to solve a problem that was never there, exactly parallel to the previous module's stock-price example: a mechanism only pays for itself when the thing it exists to solve is actually present.

contentSections.body: **Rule of thumb**: reach for retrieval when a corpus is genuinely too large to include wholesale, and which part of it is relevant depends on the specific question — not knowable in advance. Skip it when the total relevant content is small and applies to essentially every question; that's a system prompt, not a search problem. The two aren't mutually exclusive within one agent — the same internal-tools agent might have a small, always-present system prompt *and* a genuine retrieval layer over a large internal wiki, if both conditions actually hold for different parts of its job.

Retrieval earns its cost only when a corpus is genuinely too large to include wholesale and relevance can't be known in advance — small, always-relevant content is a system prompt, not a retrieval problem.

title: Chunking, and the chunk that lost its meaning
description: Why how a document is split into chunks determines whether retrieval can ever find the right thing — and the specific ways naive chunking breaks meaning.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why chunk boundaries affect whether retrieval can find relevant content at all
Diagnose a retrieval miss caused by a chunk boundary splitting meaning apart

contentSections.title: A chunk is the unit retrieval actually works with

contentSections.body: A 12-page refund policy document gets split into fixed 500-character chunks with no regard for sentence or paragraph boundaries, purely by character count. One chunk ends mid-sentence: "...refunds are available within 30 days of purchase, except for items marked final sale, which are" — and the next chunk begins "not eligible under any circumstances." A question about final-sale items retrieves the first chunk, which reads as if final-sale items *are* eligible.

contentSections.question: What's the actual defect in this chunking function, given the refund-policy example?

options.label: It splits purely by raw character count with no awareness of sentence, clause, or paragraph boundaries — so it can cut a sentence in half and separate a claim from the exception that qualifies it
500 characters is too small a chunk size — it should just be a bigger number

feedback.no-boundaries: Right. The specific failure in the example — "final sale, which are" split from "not eligible" — isn't fixed by a different number, because a purely character-count split will eventually cut *some* sentence in half no matter what size you pick. The fix is chunking on natural boundaries (sentences, paragraphs), not adjusting the character count.
feedback.wrong-size: A bigger number reduces how often a cut happens, but doesn't eliminate the actual mechanism — fixed character counts don't know where a sentence ends, so some cut will eventually land mid-clause regardless of the exact number chosen. The defect is the *method* (blind character counting), not the specific size.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A chunk is the atomic unit retrieval works with — whatever ends up in one chunk is what gets embedded, searched, and (if retrieved) handed to the model together; whatever gets split across two chunks may never be reassembled at retrieval time, because retrieval returns individual chunks, not their neighbors, by default. Splitting on raw character count treats text as an undifferentiated stream and will eventually sever a claim from the exception that changes its meaning.

contentSections.body: Chunk boundaries determine what retrieval can find together — splitting on raw character count, with no regard for sentence or paragraph structure, will eventually separate a claim from the exception that changes its meaning.

contentSections.title: Chunks that are too big lose specificity too

contentSections.body: A team, having learned not to chunk too small, swings the other way: one chunk per entire 12-page document. A question about "the final-sale exception" now retrieves the whole document — technically containing the answer, but buried among eleven other pages of unrelated policy, competing with all of that for the model's attention exactly the way last module's bloated-context lesson described.

contentSections.scenario: A chunk size decision has real trade-offs in both directions — too small (a sentence split mid-clause) and too large (a whole document as one chunk).
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine costs of chunks that are too large, specifically?

items.label: The retrieved chunk contains a lot of irrelevant material alongside the relevant part, diluting the model's attention on what actually answers the question
A single embedding vector for a whole multi-topic document has to represent all its topics at once, making it a worse match for a question about just one of them
Retrieving a few large chunks can cost more context tokens per query than retrieving several precisely-targeted small ones, even though fewer chunks were returned
Large chunks eliminate the mid-sentence splitting problem entirely, with no downside at any size

explanation.attention-dilution: Real — a chunk that's mostly irrelevant to the question still has to be attended to by the model when deciding how to use it, the same attention cost from last module's context-bloat lesson.
explanation.embedding-blur: Real — an embedding is a single vector meant to represent a chunk's meaning; a chunk spanning many topics produces a vaguer, less discriminating vector than one focused on a single topic, which hurts how well semantic search can match it to a specific question (this module's next lesson goes into embeddings directly).
explanation.cost: Real — a few 3,000-token chunks can easily cost more total tokens per query than several well-targeted 400-token chunks, even though the chunk *count* went down.
explanation.never-splits: Not true without qualification — very large chunks reduce mid-sentence splitting risk at that document's own internal boundaries, but they don't eliminate the problem in general (a document longer than the chosen chunk size still needs to be split somewhere), and they trade it for the attention-dilution and embedding-blur costs above.

contentSections.synthesis: Chunk size is a real trade-off, not a "bigger is safer" default — too small risks splitting meaning apart, too large dilutes attention and blurs the embedding's ability to discriminate one topic from another. The right size targets a coherent unit of meaning (often a section or a few paragraphs), not an arbitrary character count in either direction.

contentSections.body: In practice, a reasonable starting point for prose documents is chunks of roughly 200-500 tokens, split on paragraph or section boundaries with a small overlap — small enough that a chunk is about one coherent idea, large enough that the idea usually isn't cut in half. The right number depends on the corpus: a FAQ where each entry is a self-contained Q&A pair might chunk one entry per chunk regardless of length; a long technical manual might chunk by section heading. There's no single correct number — there's a test: **read a chunk on its own, with no neighbors. Does it make sense as a self-contained unit of meaning?** If not, the boundary is probably in the wrong place, independent of the character count.

Chunk size is a real trade-off in both directions — too small splits meaning apart, too large dilutes attention and blurs the embedding. Test a chunk by whether it reads as a coherent, self-contained unit of meaning on its own.

title: Embeddings and semantic search, mechanically
description: What an embedding actually is, how similarity search finds relevant chunks without any shared words, and where the mechanism genuinely breaks.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what an embedding vector represents and how similarity search uses it
Trace a semantic search from query to ranked results through the actual arithmetic

contentSections.title: A vector that stands in for meaning

contentSections.body: A user asks a support agent "my payment didn't go through, what happened." The most relevant help-center article is titled "Troubleshooting declined transactions" — it shares almost no words with the question ("payment" vs "transactions," "didn't go through" vs "declined"). A keyword search for the user's exact words would likely miss it. Semantic search finds it anyway.

An **embedding** is a list of numbers (a vector — typically hundreds to a few thousand dimensions) produced by a model trained so that pieces of text with similar *meaning* end up as vectors that are close together in that space, regardless of shared vocabulary. "My payment didn't go through" and "troubleshooting declined transactions" use almost no common words, but a good embedding model places their vectors close together because both are *about* the same thing: a failed payment.

```js
// conceptually — the actual numbers are opaque, only their relationships matter
embed("my payment didn't go through")        → [0.12, -0.44, 0.81, ...]  // 1536 numbers
embed("troubleshooting declined transactions") → [0.15, -0.39, 0.77, ...]  // close to the above
embed("how do I change my shipping address")  → [-0.61, 0.22, -0.05, ...] // far from both
```

Distance between two vectors — most commonly measured as **cosine similarity**, which ranges from -1 (opposite meaning) to 1 (identical meaning), ignoring vector length and comparing only direction — becomes a proxy for how semantically related two pieces of text are. This is the entire mechanism: turn text into vectors once (at indexing time), turn a query into a vector at question time, and find the corpus vectors closest to the query vector.

contentSections.scenario: Three chunk embeddings already exist: A ("declined transaction troubleshooting"), B ("how to change your shipping address"), C ("why was my card charge rejected"). A user asks: "my payment got refused, why."
contentSections.question: Semantic search ranks chunks by embedding similarity to the query, not by shared words. Which chunk should rank highest?

options.label: C — "card charge rejected" and "payment got refused" describe the same underlying event (a declined charge) even though almost no words are shared
B — because "address" and "payment" are both nouns related to an account
None of them — since no chunk contains the words "payment," "refused," or "why" verbatim

feedback.c: Right. "Card charge rejected" and "payment got refused" are near-paraphrases of the same event — a good embedding model places them close together in vector space precisely because meaning, not vocabulary overlap, is what the vectors capture.
feedback.b: Sharing a grammatical category (both nouns related to an account) isn't semantic similarity — an embedding model is trained to capture what text is actually *about*, and a shipping address change is about a completely different topic than a declined payment.
feedback.none: This is the keyword-search mistake, not the semantic-search answer — semantic search is specifically designed to find relevant content with zero shared vocabulary, which is exactly what makes it different from (and often better than) exact word matching.

contentSections.concept: Semantic search ranks by **meaning proximity in embedding space**, not word overlap — which is exactly what lets it find a relevant chunk that happens to be phrased completely differently from the query, the mechanism the next lesson's keyword-search comparison will show is also sometimes a weakness.

contentSections.body: An embedding is a vector representing meaning, not vocabulary — semantic search ranks candidates by vector closeness to the query, which is why it can find relevant content sharing almost no words with the question.

contentSections.title: The actual retrieval call, end to end

contentSections.body: All of this needs to become actual code somewhere — a real embedding call, a real index to search, and a real function an agent's tool calls at question time. Without the mechanics, "semantic search" stays an idea instead of something that returns actual chunks.

contentSections.problem: Trace a real retrieval call from a user's question to the top-3 chunks handed to the model, using Anthropic's embedding-agnostic pattern (embeddings themselves come from a dedicated embedding model, not the generation model) plus a vector store.

steps.label: Index the corpus once, offline
steps.why: This runs once per corpus (or per corpus update), not per question — the whole point of separating indexing from retrieval, from lesson one.

steps.label: Embed the incoming question
steps.why: The query has to be embedded with the *same* embedding model used to index the corpus — comparing vectors from two different embedding models is comparing numbers that don't mean the same thing.

steps.label: Search the index for nearest neighbors
steps.work:
const results = await vectorStore.query({ vector: queryVector, topK: 5 });
// results: [{ id, score: 0.87, metadata: {...} }, { id, score: 0.81, metadata: {...} }, ...]
steps.why: This returns the k chunks whose vectors are closest to the query vector, each with a similarity score — the mechanism from the first half of this lesson, executed against a real index instead of three example chunks.

steps.label: Hand only the retrieved chunks to the model
steps.why: Only the retrieved chunks — not the whole corpus — become part of this request's context, which is the entire cost benefit of retrieval over pasting everything in.

faded.problem: Same pattern, different corpus: an agent retrieving from a codebase's design docs instead of help-center articles.

blanks.prompt: What has to happen to the whole corpus before any question can be answered?
blanks.answer: it gets chunked and embedded once, offline, into a searchable index

blanks.prompt: What has to be true about the embedding model used for the query versus the one used for the corpus?
blanks.answer: it must be the same embedding model for both, or the vectors aren't comparable
accept: same model for query and corpus

blanks.prompt: What specifically gets passed to the generation model — the full corpus, or something narrower?
blanks.answer: only the top-k retrieved chunks' text, not the whole corpus

faded.why: The procedure doesn't change with the corpus's subject matter: index once, embed the query with the same model, search, hand only the retrieved slice to the model.

contentSections.procedure: 1. Chunk and embed the corpus once, offline, into a vector store. 2. Embed the incoming question with the same embedding model. 3. Query the store for the top-k nearest chunks by similarity. 4. Pass only those chunks — not the corpus — to the model as context.

contentSections.body: A real retrieval call is: index once with an embedding model, embed the query with the *same* model, search a vector store for the nearest chunks, and hand only those chunks to the generation model.

title: Keyword search that beats vectors
description: Where semantic search's strength — matching on meaning over exact words — becomes a real weakness, and why hybrid search often beats either alone.

learningObjectives.text: Identify query types where exact keyword match outperforms semantic similarity

contentSections.title: When exact words are exactly the point

contentSections.body: A developer searches an internal docs corpus for the exact error code "ERR_CONN_5502." Semantic search returns several chunks about "connection errors" and "network troubleshooting" — all thematically related to connection issues — but none of them happen to be the one specific page that documents ERR_CONN_5502 by that exact code, because the embedding model treats it as just another token in a sea of similar-sounding error-handling text.

contentSections.scenario: Semantic search found several chunks about the *general topic* of connection errors, but missed the one chunk containing the exact code being searched for.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind this specific kind of miss?

options.label: An embedding model captures general topical meaning, which makes it comparatively weak at distinguishing one exact identifier, code, or rare term from other text that's topically similar but not the same identifier
The embedding model wasn't trained on error codes at all
This is a chunking problem, not a search-method problem

feedback.topical-not-exact: Right. Embeddings are good at capturing what text is generally *about* — exactly the strength from the previous lesson — but that same strength means an exact code, ID, or rare term can get "smoothed over" into the general topic it appears in, rather than treated as the precise, distinguishing token it actually is for this kind of query.
feedback.untrained: Not really the mechanism — this isn't about the model never having seen error-code-shaped text; it's a structural property of what embeddings represent (topical meaning) versus what this query needs (an exact match on one specific string).
feedback.chunking: Chunking quality matters generally, but even a perfectly chunked corpus has this problem — the issue is that semantic similarity treats "ERR_CONN_5502" as topically close to other connection-error text, not as a unique, exact string to match precisely.

contentSections.mechanism: Exact identifiers — error codes, product SKUs, function names, ticket numbers, legal citations — are cases where what the user needs is a precise string match, not a topical neighbor. Semantic search, built to find things that mean the same thing even with different words, is comparatively weak exactly where the difference between two strings (ERR_CONN_5502 vs ERR_CONN_5501) matters enormously and their *topic* is nearly identical.

contentSections.body:
**Keyword search** (often BM25, a classic ranking algorithm scoring documents by exact term frequency and rarity) doesn't have this problem — it matches "ERR_CONN_5502" as a literal string, and a document containing that exact code ranks highly regardless of how it's phrased around it. Its weakness is the mirror image of semantic search's strength: a keyword search for "payment didn't go through" would likely miss "troubleshooting declined transactions," because it shares almost no literal words with the query — exactly the case semantic search from the previous lesson handled well.

Neither method dominates the other; they fail in opposite, complementary places.

Semantic search is comparatively weak on exact identifiers and rare precise strings — codes, IDs, exact names — because it captures topical meaning, not literal string matching, which is exactly where keyword search is strong.

contentSections.title: Hybrid search: running both and combining results

contentSections.body: A team, after hitting the ERR_CONN_5502 problem, considers switching entirely from semantic to keyword search. That fixes the error-code case and immediately reintroduces the "payment didn't go through" problem from the start of this lesson — trading one blind spot for its exact opposite.

contentSections.intro: Design a hybrid search that gets both the error-code case and the paraphrased-question case right.

fields.prompt: Which search methods should run against the corpus for each incoming query?

options.label: Only whichever method the team's existing infrastructure already supports
Both semantic search and keyword search, run in parallel for every query

feedback.one: Committing to one method locks in that method's specific blind spot — semantic-only misses exact codes, keyword-only misses paraphrases. Neither is a full solution alone.
feedback.both: Right — running both in parallel means an exact-code query gets caught by keyword search even if semantic search misses it, and a paraphrased query gets caught by semantic search even if keyword search misses it.

fields.prompt: How should the two result sets be combined into one ranked list?

options.label: Use whichever method returned more results for this particular query
Merge and re-rank both result sets using a combined score (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion), so a chunk that scores well on either method surfaces

feedback.pick-one: This just relocates the same problem — picking one method's results per query still means whichever method you didn't pick could have found something the other missed.
feedback.merge-score: Right — a proper fusion step lets a chunk that ranks well on keyword match (the error code) or well on semantic similarity (the paraphrase) both surface in the final list, rather than one method's blind spot silently winning.

fields.prompt: If a query is a bare exact identifier (like a ticket number), should hybrid search still run semantic search at all?

options.label: Skip semantic search for obviously identifier-shaped queries, since it's unlikely to contribute usefully and costs an extra embedding call
Always run both regardless of query shape, for consistency

feedback.skip: A defensible optimization — an obviously identifier-shaped query (matches a known ID pattern) gains little from semantic search and paying for the extra embedding call and merge step is pure overhead in that specific case. This is a genuine efficiency call, not a correctness requirement either way.
feedback.always: Not wrong exactly, but it's the less efficient default — a query that's transparently just an exact code gets essentially no benefit from a semantic pass, so always running both regardless of query shape trades a small efficiency loss for simplicity, which is a defensible but not obviously better choice than the targeted skip.

contentSections.synthesis: Hybrid search runs semantic and keyword search in parallel, combines and re-ranks both result sets so a chunk strong on either dimension can surface, and can skip the semantic pass as an optimization for obviously identifier-shaped queries. This covers both failure modes from this lesson without requiring the corpus or the query to declare in advance which kind of match it needs.

contentSections.body: Hybrid search — running semantic and keyword search in parallel and merging the ranked results — covers both failure modes at once: exact identifiers that semantic search smooths over, and paraphrases that keyword search misses.

title: Evaluating retrieval separately from generation
description: Why a good final answer doesn't prove retrieval worked — and how to measure precision and recall on retrieval alone, isolated from what the model does afterward.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a correct final answer doesn't confirm retrieval found the right chunks
Design a retrieval-only evaluation using precision and recall against a labeled query set

contentSections.title: A right answer can hide a wrong retrieval

contentSections.body: A RAG-based support agent gets a question right: "is final-sale merchandise refundable?" — "No, final-sale items are not eligible for refunds." The team ships, satisfied. What nobody checked: the retrieval step actually returned three unrelated chunks about shipping times, and the model answered correctly from its own general training knowledge about typical retail policy, not from anything retrieved. The next question, about a policy specific to this company that isn't common industry knowledge, gets a confident, wrong answer — and nobody can tell from the first success that retrieval was never actually contributing.

contentSections.scenario: The correct answer to the final-sale question happened even though retrieval returned nothing relevant.
contentSections.question: What does this reveal about judging a RAG system purely by whether final answers look correct?

options.label: A correct final answer conflates two separate things — whether retrieval found the right material, and whether the model produced a good answer — and a model can get the second right without the first, especially on questions its training data already covers
Nothing — if the final answer is right, the system is working correctly by definition
This proves the model is always more reliable than retrieval and retrieval can be skipped

feedback.conflates: Right. End-to-end correctness is the sum of two different systems working (or not): retrieval finding the right chunks, and generation using them well. A model's own general knowledge can paper over a retrieval failure on questions that happen to be common knowledge — which is exactly why this specific failure is invisible until a question comes along where general knowledge isn't enough and there's nothing correct to fall back on.
feedback.fine: This is exactly the trap the hook describes — judging only by whether the final answer sounds right missed a retrieval system that was completely failing, because generation quietly covered for it on this particular question.
feedback.skip-retrieval: The opposite conclusion from what the scenario supports — the very next question in the hook is where skipping retrieval would fail badly, precisely because it needs company-specific information no general training data would contain. The lesson here is to measure retrieval, not to abandon it.

contentSections.mechanism: A RAG system's final answer quality is a product of two separable stages: retrieval quality (did the search find the right chunks) and generation quality (did the model use what it was given well). Testing only the combined output can't distinguish "retrieval worked and generation used it well" from "retrieval failed but generation happened to know the answer anyway" — and the second case is a silent time bomb that only detonates on a question the model can't answer from general knowledge alone.

contentSections.body: A correct final answer doesn't confirm retrieval worked — generation can paper over a retrieval failure using general knowledge, invisibly, until a question comes along with nothing to fall back on. Evaluate retrieval on its own, against a labeled query set.

contentSections.title: Precision and recall for retrieval, computed

contentSections.body: With a labeled eval set in hand, "is retrieval good" still needs to become a number, not a feeling — otherwise a change to chunking or the embedding model has no honest way to be compared against what came before it.

contentSections.scenario: For the query "how long do refunds take to process," the labeled correct chunks are {chunk-3, chunk-4}. Retrieval with top-k=5 actually returns {chunk-3, chunk-9, chunk-4, chunk-12, chunk-1}.
contentSections.question: Precision is the fraction of *retrieved* chunks that were actually relevant. What's the precision here, as a percentage?
contentSections.explanation: 2 of the 5 retrieved chunks (chunk-3 and chunk-4) are in the relevant set — 2/5 = 40%. The other 3 retrieved chunks (chunk-9, chunk-12, chunk-1) are irrelevant noise mixed into the top-5 results, exactly the attention-dilution cost the chunking lesson named — a low-precision retrieval hands the model more noise to sift through even when it does contain the right answer.

contentSections.body: Precision (how much of what was retrieved is relevant) and recall (how much of what's relevant was retrieved) are two separate, sometimes trading-off numbers — both computed against a labeled eval set, and both needed to know whether retrieval is actually working.

title: Diagnose eight retrieval failures
description: Eight drills applying this module's full toolkit — when retrieval is the right tool, chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, and precision/recall evaluation — to new retrieval failures.

learningObjectives.text: Apply retrieval-scope, chunking, embedding, hybrid-search, and evaluation judgment to new scenarios

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — this is the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against retrieval failures you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: before trusting a RAG system, ask whether retrieval is actually needed here, whether chunks preserve meaning, whether the search method matches the query shape, and whether you've measured retrieval's own precision and recall — not just whether the final answers sound right.

title: Build and evaluate a retrieval layer
description: Build a real retrieval layer over a corpus of your own, with deliberate chunking, and measure its precision and recall against a labeled query set you build yourself.

learningObjectives.text: Build, chunk, index, and evaluate a retrieval layer with measured precision and recall on a self-built query set

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Everything in this module was building toward one working thing: a real retrieval layer over a real corpus, with chunking decisions you made deliberately, and honest, measured precision and recall — not an assumption that it's probably fine because the demo questions came back looking right.

contentSections.title: A retrieval layer with measured precision and recall
contentSections.brief: Pick a real corpus you have access to — documentation for a tool you use, a set of your own notes, a public dataset of articles, or similar — with at least 15-20 distinct documents or sections. Chunk it deliberately (not by arbitrary character count), embed and index it, and build a query interface that returns the top-k relevant chunks for a question. Then build your own labeled query set of at least 10 questions with hand-identified correct chunks, and compute real precision and recall against it.
contentSections.deliverable: The indexing and retrieval code, your chunking strategy and why you chose it for this specific corpus, the 10+ query labeled eval set with the correct chunks identified by hand, and a precision/recall report per query and averaged — plus one specific retrieval failure you found and diagnosed (which lesson's failure mode it matches, and what you'd change).

stages.title: Choose the corpus and chunk it deliberately
stages.instructions: Pick a real corpus with real internal structure (sections, paragraphs, natural units — not an undifferentiated blob of text). Write a chunker that respects that structure, per lesson two's test: does each chunk read as a coherent, self-contained unit of meaning on its own? Document your chunk size choice and why it fits this specific corpus.
stages.checkpoint: A chunked corpus where you can point to specific chunks and explain why the boundaries land where they do.

stages.title: Embed and index
stages.instructions: Embed every chunk with a real embedding model and store the vectors in a searchable index (a vector database, or even an in-memory cosine-similarity search over a small corpus is fine for this lab's scale). Confirm the query-time embedding call uses the exact same model as indexing.
stages.checkpoint: A working index you can query with an arbitrary question and get back ranked chunks with similarity scores.

stages.title: Build the labeled eval set and measure
stages.instructions: Write at least 10 real questions someone would plausibly ask this corpus, including at least one exact-identifier-style query if your corpus has any (a specific term, code, or name) and at least one paraphrase-style query. For each, hand-identify which chunk(s) should be retrieved by reading the source material yourself — not by looking at what your system currently returns. Run your retrieval system against all 10+ queries and compute precision and recall per query and averaged, per lesson five's formulas.
stages.checkpoint: A precision/recall report against a genuinely independently-labeled eval set — the labels come from reading the source, not from what the system happened to return.

stages.title: Diagnose one real failure
stages.instructions: Find at least one query in your eval set where retrieval performed worse than expected (low precision, low recall, or missing an obviously relevant chunk). Diagnose which specific failure mode from this module it matches — a chunk boundary problem, an embedding weakness on an exact term, or something else — and describe the specific fix you'd apply.
stages.checkpoint: One concrete diagnosed failure, named against a specific lesson's mechanism, with a specific proposed fix — not a vague 'retrieval could be better.'

rubric.meets: Correct chunks were identified by reading the source material directly, not by looking at what the retrieval system already returns.

rubric.criterion: Precision and recall are both computed and reported
rubric.meets: Both metrics are calculated per query and averaged across the full eval set, using the formulas from lesson five, not a single vague 'accuracy' number.

rubric.criterion: The eval set covers more than one query type
rubric.meets: At least one exact-identifier-style query and one paraphrase-style query are both present, testing both failure modes from this module.

rubric.meets: A genuine underperforming query is traced to a specific mechanism from this module (chunking, embedding weakness, etc.), not left as an unexplained low number.

contentSections.body: A retrieval layer only counts as evaluated when precision and recall are measured against an independently-labeled query set — not when the demo questions happen to come back looking right.

options.label: A selection problem — finding the small relevant slice of a corpus too large to include wholesale, when relevance can't be known in advance
A context-window-size problem, solved by using the largest available model
A formatting problem — making a large document more readable

options.label: It can cut a sentence or clause in half, separating a claim from the exception that qualifies it, since it ignores natural boundaries
Fixed character counts always produce chunks that are too large
It has no real risk as long as the character count is a round number

Semantic search actually does require shared words, just fewer of them than keyword search
