questions.prompt: Why does an agent's per-call cost climb over a long run even when each user message is short?

options.label: The API is stateless — the full message history is resent and rebilled on every call
The model computes more slowly as conversations get longer
It's a provider billing bug

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here: this module's indexing-versus-per-query split (lesson one) exploits the same stateless-API reality by moving expensive work offline.

questions.prompt: What's the test for whether content should be always-present in context versus fetched on demand?

options.label: Whether it would change the next action on every single step, regardless of what that step is about
Whether it's technically possible to fit it in the window
Whether it was written recently

questions.explanation: The same test this module's first lesson used to distinguish a genuine retrieval problem from a simple named-lookup case.

questions.prompt: Why does a hard constraint buried in the middle of a long system prompt tend to get missed?

options.label: Attention across a long context is uneven — content at the start and end tends to be weighted more than a long undifferentiated middle
The wording is usually unclear in practice
Models ignore any instruction after a fixed sentence count

questions.explanation: The lost-in-the-middle effect — relevant again here, since a retrieved chunk's position in the assembled context matters the same way.

questions.prompt: What should a compaction step extract from older conversation history?

options.label: Concrete decisions with specific values, and still-open questions — not a narrative summary
A pleasant-sounding overall progress summary
The complete raw output of every tool call

questions.explanation: The same specific-over-narrative discipline this module's chunking lesson applies to what a chunk should preserve.

questions.prompt: Per that module, what's the useful move once a step fails, beyond just noting that it failed?

options.label: Tracing the failure to the specific assumption it contradicts, because that determines whether retrying could possibly help
Retrying the same step immediately with the same inputs
Reporting only that the step failed, with no further diagnosis

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here: this module's retrieval-failure diagnosis (in the lab and practice set) applies the same discipline — trace a low score to its specific mechanism, not just note that it's low.

questions.prompt: What makes a report of what changed during a run genuinely honest, per that module's last lesson?

options.label: Naming the specific assumption that broke, the specific action taken, and what's still uncertain — not a clean-sounding summary of the end state
A confident statement that everything ultimately worked out
Omitting anything that didn't go as planned, to keep the report simple

questions.explanation: The same honesty standard this module's evaluation lesson demands of a retrieval report — real precision/recall numbers, including the weak ones, not a summary that smooths over what didn't work.

contentSections.body: If these mostly landed, the retrieval-scope, chunking, embedding, and evaluation vocabulary is solid enough to build the next module's long-term memory skills on top of.

title: What is actually worth remembering
description: Telling a durable fact worth persisting across sessions apart from transient state that should die with the session — and the real retrieval cost of storing everything just in case.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish durable, cross-session-worthy facts from transient, session-scoped state
Explain why storing every exchange as long-term memory degrades retrieval quality later

contentSections.title: Would this matter in a different, later conversation?

contentSections.body: A coding assistant is wired to store every user message as a "memory" so it can "remember the user" across sessions. By month two it has over 40,000 stored entries: "user is currently debugging a null pointer in checkout.js," "user asked what time it is," "user prefers tabs over spaces," "the API call just now returned a 500." One of these is worth knowing three months from now. The other three thousand aren't.

contentSections.scenario: Four things said during one session with the coding assistant: (1) "I prefer tabs over spaces," (2) "I'm currently on step 3 of setting up this webhook," (3) "the API call just returned a 500," (4) "I always want unit tests written before implementation, not after."
contentSections.question: Which of these are durable facts worth writing to long-term memory, versus transient state that should die with the session?

options.label: (1) and (4) are durable preferences that will matter in a future, unrelated session; (2) and (3) are transient state specific to this session that resolves or becomes irrelevant once the session ends
All four are worth storing — more remembered context can only help
None are worth storing — an agent should treat every session as independent

feedback.correct: Right. (1) and (4) are stable preferences that apply regardless of what specific task is happening — genuinely useful three months from now in a completely different task. (2) is a snapshot of where this specific session's task stood, meaningless once that task either finishes or is abandoned. (3) is an already-resolved transient error with no future relevance.
feedback.all: This is exactly the failure mode from the hook — "more context can only help" is what produced 40,000 mostly-useless entries. Transient state doesn't help a future session; it adds noise a later retrieval has to filter through, which the second half of this lesson gets into directly.
feedback.none: Too extreme in the other direction — a real preference like "unit tests before implementation" genuinely should persist and change how future sessions behave; treating every session as fully independent throws away real, durable signal along with the noise.

contentSections.concept: The test: **would this matter in a different, later conversation that doesn't share this session's specific context?** A preference, a standing decision, a stable fact about the user or the project — yes. A snapshot of where a specific task currently stands, or an error that's already been resolved — no, because it's meaningless once this session's specific thread of work ends.

contentSections.body: This mirrors a distinction the previous module drew for context within a single run — always-present versus fetch-on-demand — but at a longer timescale: **durable versus transient** is the same kind of test applied across sessions instead of across steps. A durable fact is worth the permanent cost of storing and later retrieving it. A transient fact isn't wrong to have known in the moment; it's just not worth carrying forward once its moment has passed.

A durable memory would matter in a different, later conversation with no shared context — a preference, a standing decision, a stable fact. Transient state — where a specific task currently stands, an already-resolved error — shouldn't survive past the session it happened in.

contentSections.title: The cost of storing everything, just in case

contentSections.body: Six months into the 40,000-entry memory store, a user asks the coding assistant a genuine question about their testing preferences. Retrieval searches the memory index and returns a mix: the one real preference entry, buried among a dozen semantically similar-sounding but irrelevant entries — old debugging snapshots that happen to mention "test" somewhere, resolved errors from unrelated projects, small talk.

contentSections.scenario: The genuinely relevant preference entry is technically still in the memory store and technically retrievable — but it's now one signal among thousands of mostly-irrelevant entries competing for the same retrieval slots.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism connecting "we stored everything" to "retrieval quality got worse"?

options.label: Every unnecessary stored entry is more corpus noise a later retrieval has to search and rank against — exactly the precision cost from the previous module's retrieval lessons, just applied to a memory store instead of a document corpus
Nothing changed — the relevant entry is still there and still retrievable, so retrieval quality is unaffected by how much else is stored
The memory store simply reached a hard capacity limit and started silently dropping entries

feedback.noise: Right. A long-term memory store is a corpus, and everything the previous module said about retrieval precision applies to it directly: every low-value entry stored is one more candidate a similarity search has to rank against, diluting precision the same way an oversized or poorly chunked document corpus did. Storing everything 'just in case' isn't free — it's paid for later, in every subsequent retrieval.
feedback.no-effect: Being technically present isn't the same as being reliably found near the top of a ranked result set — the previous module's precision metric exists precisely because "it's in there somewhere" doesn't guarantee a search surfaces it cleanly among thousands of other candidates.
feedback.capacity: Nothing in the scenario suggests a capacity limit was hit — the mechanism is about retrieval quality degrading as noise accumulates, not about entries being dropped or lost.

contentSections.mechanism: A memory store is retrieved from using the same similarity-search mechanics as any other corpus. Every entry stored — useful or not — is a candidate that competes for ranking on every future query. Writing indiscriminately doesn't just cost storage; it directly degrades the precision of every future retrieval against that store, for exactly the reasons the previous module's precision metric was built to catch.

contentSections.body: This is the concrete reason "what's worth remembering" isn't a philosophical question — it's a load-bearing engineering decision that determines whether a memory store stays useful or slowly drowns in its own history. The discipline this module builds toward: write only what passes the durability test from the first half of this lesson, and — the next lesson goes into this directly — make that decision deliberately, not as a side effect of logging everything that happens.
A memory store is retrieved from like any other corpus — every low-value entry stored is noise that degrades every future retrieval's precision, not a free hedge against forgetting something useful.

title: Writing memory deliberately, not automatically
description: Turning the durability test into an explicit write decision — a real memory-write function with a stated trigger and a structured schema, instead of logging everything by default.

learningObjectives.text: Design an explicit trigger for when a memory-write decision should fire
Structure a memory entry with fields that support later retrieval and resolution

contentSections.title: A write is a decision, not a side effect of logging

contentSections.body: The 40,000-entry memory store from lesson one wasn't the result of a bad rule about *what* to remember — there was no rule at all. Every turn of every conversation got appended to memory automatically, as a side effect of the conversation happening, with nobody and nothing ever asking whether this particular turn passed the durability test.

contentSections.scenario: Redesigning the write path: instead of logging every turn, a memory-write only happens when something specific triggers it.
contentSections.question: Which of these are legitimate triggers for a deliberate memory write?

items.label: The user explicitly states a standing preference ("I always want...", "never do X")
The user corrects a belief the agent previously held or acted on
A decision was made that will constrain future work in this project (an architecture choice, a naming convention adopted)
Every user message, by default, regardless of content
A routine tool call that succeeded exactly as expected, with nothing notable about the result

explanation.explicit-pref: Legitimate — this is exactly the durable-preference case from lesson one, and it's usually explicit enough in the user's own words to detect reliably.
explanation.correction: Legitimate, and important — a correction means an old belief (possibly already stored) needs to be updated, which the next lessons in this module deal with directly.
explanation.durable-decision: Legitimate — a project-level decision that constrains future work passes the same durability test as a personal preference, just scoped to a project instead of a person.
explanation.every-turn: Not legitimate as a default — this is the exact mechanism that produced the 40,000-entry store from lesson one, storing transient state indiscriminately.
explanation.tool-success: Not legitimate on its own — a routine, expected tool result carries no new durable information; it's already served its purpose the moment it informed whatever decision came next.

contentSections.synthesis: A deliberate write path fires on specific, recognizable triggers — an explicit preference, a correction, a durable decision — not on the mere fact that a turn happened. This turns memory-writing from an automatic side effect into a judgment call made at a specific, checkable moment.

contentSections.body: A memory write should fire on specific, recognizable triggers — an explicit preference, a correction, a durable decision — evaluated as a real decision at write time, not appended automatically as a side effect of the conversation happening.

contentSections.title: Getting the trigger's boundary right

contentSections.body: A team implements "write to memory whenever the user says something personal." It works for the intended case — "I prefer async communication over calls" gets stored correctly — and also stores "I'm feeling a bit tired today" and "my favorite color is blue," neither of which will ever change what the agent should do differently in a future session.

contentSections.question: What's the actual defect in this trigger, given what happened with "I'm feeling a bit tired today"?

options.label: "Personal" is the wrong category — it catches content that's about the person without asking whether it's durable and actionable for a future session, which is the actual test from lesson one
The classify() call itself is unreliable and should be replaced with a keyword list

feedback.wrong-category: Right. "Personal" and "durable and actionable" are different properties — a mood statement is personal but not durable; a preference about communication style is both. The trigger asked the wrong question, so it correctly caught personal content while incorrectly treating personalness as a proxy for worth-remembering.
feedback.unreliable: The reliability of the classification call isn't the issue described — the problem is what it was asked to classify. Asking a more reliable version of "is this personal" would still store mood statements; the category itself needs to change, not the reliability of detecting it.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A trigger needs to ask the actual durability question directly — would this matter in a different, later conversation — not a proxy question like "is this personal" that happens to correlate with it sometimes but also catches a lot that doesn't pass the real test.

contentSections.body: The fix is asking the durability question directly, as the code example in the first half of this lesson does — "a standing preference, a correction, or a durable decision" — rather than a loosely related proxy like "personal." This is worth testing deliberately: run the trigger against a set of real example messages, some that should store and some that shouldn't, and check the boundary lands where lesson one's test says it should, before trusting it in production.

A write trigger has to ask the actual durability question — would this matter in a different session — not a loosely correlated proxy like "is this personal," which catches genuine preferences and pure mood chatter alike.

title: Retrieving the memory that's relevant now
description: Why topical similarity alone retrieves stale memories over more relevant recent ones, and how to scope retrieval to the current context instead of anything that merely matches.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why pure similarity search can retrieve a stale memory over a more relevant recent one
Design a memory retrieval that combines similarity, recency, and scope

contentSections.title: Similar isn't the same as current

contentSections.body: A user asks their coding assistant "what's my testing preference again?" Memory retrieval, ranked purely by semantic similarity, surfaces a memory from eight months ago: "I prefer minimal test coverage, just the critical paths." A more recent memory — three weeks old — says the opposite: "I've changed my mind, I want full coverage on anything touching payments now." Both are similarly worded and similarly "about testing," so pure similarity ranks them close together, and the stale one happens to rank slightly higher.

contentSections.scenario: Both memories are topically about testing preferences and score similarly on semantic similarity to the query. One is current; one is eight months stale.
contentSections.question: What's missing from a retrieval that ranks purely by similarity?

options.label: Similarity alone has no concept of time — it treats an eight-month-old and a three-week-old memory as equally valid candidates if they're equally similar in wording, with nothing to prefer the more recent, more likely current one
The embedding model needs to be retrained on more recent data
Nothing is actually wrong — both are valid preferences and should both be surfaced

feedback.no-recency: Right. Semantic similarity measures topical closeness, not currency. Two contradictory statements about the same topic can be equally 'similar' to a query about that topic — similarity alone gives no signal about which one is more likely to still be true.
feedback.retrain: This isn't a model-training problem — it's a structural gap in what pure similarity search measures. No amount of retraining an embedding model teaches it that newer facts tend to supersede older ones on the same topic; that's a property retrieval logic has to add, not something embeddings inherently encode.
feedback.both-valid: Surfacing both without resolution just pushes the contradiction onto the model reading them, with no signal about which one is current — which is exactly the contradiction-handling problem the next lesson deals with directly, but retrieval ranking should already be doing better than treating them as equally likely true.

contentSections.mechanism: Semantic similarity search, unmodified, has no built-in notion of time — it was never designed to. A memory retrieval system needs recency as a *second* signal alongside similarity, because the corpus it searches (unlike a static document set) is one where facts genuinely change over time and older entries on the same topic can become actively wrong, not just less relevant.

contentSections.body: Pure similarity has no concept of time — a stale and a current memory on the same topic can score equally well. A real memory-retrieval score blends similarity with a recency factor, weighted to how fast that kind of fact actually changes.

contentSections.title: Scoped to the current context, not anything that matches

contentSections.body: A user working on Project B asks their assistant a question. Memory retrieval, searching across the assistant's entire memory store, surfaces a semantically similar-sounding preference the user stated months ago — but it was said specifically about Project A, and doesn't apply here. Nothing about the retrieval flagged that the memory came from an unrelated context.

contentSections.scenario: A memory-retrieval call for a question inside Project B's workspace.
contentSections.question: Which of these should narrow or filter what's eligible for retrieval, beyond similarity and recency alone?

items.label: A project or workspace tag on each memory, so cross-project retrieval requires an explicit decision, not an accident
The memory's type (preference, correction, decision) — some queries only want one kind
Which user the memory belongs to, in any multi-user system
Nothing beyond raw similarity — any metadata filtering risks missing something relevant

explanation.project-scope: Real — scoping to the relevant project by default (with cross-project surfaced only deliberately, if ever useful) prevents exactly the Project A preference leaking into Project B's context.
explanation.memory-type: Real — a query specifically about "what did we decide about the API design" benefits from filtering to decision-type memories rather than ranking preferences and corrections equally alongside them.
explanation.user-scope: Real, and the highest-stakes one — this becomes a genuine privacy boundary in a multi-user system, which the last lesson of this module deals with directly.
explanation.raw-similarity-only: This is the exact failure from the hook — 'might miss something relevant' is a real risk on the margin, but unscoped retrieval actively surfaces genuinely irrelevant (and, worse, potentially cross-user) content with no filter at all, which is a bigger and more concrete cost.

contentSections.synthesis: A working memory retrieval filters by scope (project, user) before or alongside ranking by similarity and recency — narrowing the candidate pool to what's actually eligible for this context, not searching the entire store and hoping similarity alone sorts it out.

contentSections.body: Scope — project, user, memory type — should filter the candidate pool before ranking by similarity and recency, not be left to hope similarity alone sorts out what's actually relevant to this context.

title: Contradiction, staleness and forgetting
description: What happens when a new memory contradicts an old one — and a real forgetting policy that resolves and expires memory instead of accumulating it indefinitely.

learningObjectives.text: Design a contradiction-handling step that resolves conflicting memories instead of storing both indefinitely
Distinguish memory categories that need an expiry policy from ones that don't

contentSections.title: When a new memory contradicts an old one

contentSections.body: An agent recommends a user's old employer's internal tool in a work-related suggestion, six months after the user mentioned changing jobs. The job-change fact was stored. So was the old employer's tooling preference. Nothing at write time checked whether the new fact contradicted anything already stored — both memories just sat there, and retrieval had no way to know one had quietly made the other wrong.

contentSections.scenario: The memory store append-only logs every write. The job-change memory and the old-employer-tooling memory are both present, unrelated at write time, both still retrievable.
contentSections.question: What's missing from a purely append-only memory-write path?

options.label: A check, at write time, for existing memories the new one might contradict or supersede — without it, old and new facts coexist indefinitely with no signal about which is current
Nothing — append-only is the correct design, and contradiction should be resolved at retrieval time instead
The job-change fact should never have been written in the first place

feedback.no-check: Right. Append-only logging (useful for an audit trail) without any contradiction check means the store accumulates facts that may actively conflict, with nothing marking which one is current. The write path needs to check against existing related memories, not just add to the pile.
feedback.retrieval-time-only: Deferring resolution entirely to retrieval time is possible but expensive — it means every future retrieval has to independently re-detect and re-resolve the same contradiction, repeatedly, instead of resolving it once at the moment the new information arrives.
feedback.shouldnt-write: The job-change fact is exactly the kind of durable, correction-triggering write from lesson two — it should absolutely be written. The gap isn't that it was written; it's that writing it didn't trigger a check against what it contradicts.

contentSections.mechanism: A write step should check for existing memories on the same subject before simply appending — and when a genuine contradiction is found, resolve it explicitly (mark the old one superseded, keep both for audit purposes but change which one retrieval prefers) rather than leaving two contradictory facts to compete equally at every future retrieval.

contentSections.body: A memory write should check for contradiction against existing related memories and mark the old one superseded, rather than letting old and new facts accumulate side by side with no signal about which is current.

contentSections.title: Explicit forgetting, not indefinite accumulation

contentSections.body: Even with contradiction resolution in place, a memory store keeps every superseded entry, every transient-adjacent edge case that slipped past the write trigger, and every fact — durable or not — forever, on the theory that deleting anything risks losing something useful someday.

contentSections.intro: Design a forgetting policy that handles three different kinds of memory correctly.

fields.prompt: What should happen to a memory marked supersededBy an updated fact?

options.label: Keep it in storage (for audit trail) but exclude it from normal retrieval by default
Delete it immediately once superseded

feedback.keep-hidden: Right — this preserves the audit trail from the previous pod (useful for understanding how a belief changed over time, or for accountability) while still keeping it out of normal retrieval, which is what actually matters for retrieval quality.
feedback.delete: Immediate deletion loses the audit trail for no retrieval benefit — excluding it from retrieval already solves the noise problem; deletion is a separate decision that should be driven by an explicit policy or request, not by supersession alone.

fields.prompt: What about a memory type that's inherently time-bound (e.g. "user is currently traveling until March 15") that was mistakenly written as durable?

options.label: Give it an explicit expiresAt field and stop retrieving it (or actively delete it) once that date passes
Leave it in the store indefinitely, since it was already written as durable

feedback.expiry: Right — a fact that's true only within a known window should carry that window explicitly, so it stops being retrieved (or gets cleaned up entirely) once it's no longer true, rather than becoming stale noise the way the job-change/old-tooling case did.
feedback.forever: Treating it as durable forever is exactly how a temporary fact becomes a stale, silently-wrong one later — the fix isn't to leave it be, it's to recognize it belongs to a category that should have carried an expiry from the start.

fields.prompt: What about a genuinely permanent fact, like the user's name or a foundational architecture decision that hasn't changed in years?

options.label: No expiry — it stays retrievable indefinitely unless explicitly corrected or superseded
Give it an expiry anyway, for consistency with other memory types

feedback.no-expiry: Right — not every memory needs a forgetting mechanism; a genuinely stable fact should persist until something actually contradicts it, and forcing an artificial expiry on it would just mean re-deriving or re-confirming something that never actually changed.
feedback.force-expiry: Forcing expiry on stable facts for consistency creates busywork with no benefit — the point of a forgetting policy is to match the mechanism to the fact's actual lifespan, not to apply one mechanism uniformly regardless of whether it fits.

contentSections.synthesis: A real forgetting policy isn't one rule — it's three: superseded facts get excluded from retrieval but kept for audit, time-bound facts carry an explicit expiry and clean up automatically, and genuinely stable facts persist with no expiry until something actually contradicts them. Applying the same rule to all three either loses history that mattered or keeps noise that shouldn't have persisted.

contentSections.body: A forgetting policy needs to match the memory's actual lifespan: superseded facts hidden but audit-preserved, time-bound facts explicitly expiring, stable facts persisting with no expiry at all — not one uniform rule applied to all three.

title: Memory as a privacy question
description: Why persisted memory about a real person is a privacy boundary, not just an engineering convenience — cross-user isolation, and what a genuine deletion request actually has to touch.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the mechanism by which unscoped memory storage becomes a cross-user privacy failure
Design a deletion path that actually removes a memory from every place it's stored, not just its primary record

contentSections.title: A memory store is a store of facts about real people

contentSections.body: A support agent's memory index stores preferences and personal details from every customer, indexed in one shared vector store with no per-customer isolation key. A misconfigured query — one that forgets to apply the user-scope filter from lesson three — retrieves and surfaces Customer A's stored medical-related note into a conversation with Customer B. Nobody wrote malicious code; the isolation simply wasn't structural.

contentSections.scenario: The retrieval bug was a missing filter parameter in one code path, not a deliberate design choice to share data across users.
contentSections.question: What made this kind of failure possible in the first place?

options.label: Isolation between users' memories was enforced by remembering to apply a filter correctly every time, rather than being structural — a missing filter in any one code path becomes a real cross-user data leak
Vector databases are inherently insecure and shouldn't be used for anything containing personal information
This was a one-off coding mistake with no general lesson to draw from it

feedback.not-structural: Right. When user isolation depends on every query correctly remembering to pass a filter, it's only as safe as the least careful code path that queries the store — one missed filter anywhere is a real leak. The fix is making isolation structural (separate indexes per user, or a filter enforced at the storage layer itself, not just conventionally applied by each caller).
feedback.vector-db-insecure: The technology isn't the source of the risk — the same missing-filter mistake is possible in a relational database too. The lesson is about how isolation is enforced (structurally versus by convention), not about which storage technology is used.
feedback.single-bug: This is exactly the kind of failure worth generalizing from — 'remembering to add a filter every time' is a fragile isolation strategy regardless of which specific code path happens to forget it first; the general lesson is to make isolation impossible to accidentally skip.

contentSections.mechanism: Cross-user isolation that depends on every caller correctly applying a scope filter is only as strong as the most careless query in the codebase. Structural isolation — separate storage per tenant, or a filter enforced at the data-access layer so it's impossible to accidentally omit — turns a "we should remember to filter" convention into a guarantee that doesn't depend on every developer getting every query right, every time.

contentSections.body: This connects directly back to lesson three's scoping filter — the difference here is what's at stake when scoping fails. A retrieval miss on an unrelated project is an annoyance; a retrieval leak of one customer's personal data into another customer's session is a real privacy incident, potentially a legally significant one depending on what was stored and where the users are located. That difference in stakes is exactly why isolation for a memory store holding real personal information deserves to be enforced structurally, not left to consistent discipline across every query in the codebase.

User isolation enforced by remembering to filter correctly is only as safe as the least careful query in the codebase — for a memory store holding real personal data, isolation needs to be structural, not conventional.

contentSections.title: What a real deletion request has to touch

contentSections.body: A user asks the agent, "please forget that I mentioned my health condition." The team's engineer deletes the row from the primary memory-store table and reports back "done." The same content, however, still exists in the embedding index (a separate store, queried independently), in a backup taken the night before, and in a compacted summary written weeks ago that folded the health mention into a broader paragraph about the user's context.

contentSections.scenario: The team's deletion touched only the primary record's row.
contentSections.question: Which of these does a genuine deletion request need to actually reach for the request to be honestly fulfilled?

items.label: The primary memory record
The corresponding vector in the embedding index used for retrieval
Any compacted or summarized memory that folded the deleted content into a broader entry
Backups containing the record, on whatever retention schedule and process applies to them
Nothing beyond the primary record — once it's gone from the main table, the request is fulfilled

explanation.primary-row: Necessary but, as the hook shows, not sufficient on its own — it's only one of several places the same content lives.
explanation.vector-index: A separate store from the primary record in most real architectures — deleting the primary row doesn't automatically remove the corresponding vector, which can still be retrieved and surfaced even after the 'source' record is gone.
explanation.derived-summaries: Easy to miss — a compaction step (this module's second-lesson-adjacent concern, extended from context compaction to memory) can have folded the sensitive content into a broader summary that survives deletion of the original entry entirely.
explanation.backups: Real, and often the hardest — a genuine deletion policy has to define what happens to backups, since 'delete it everywhere except the backup we happen to restore from next month' isn't actually deletion.
explanation.nothing-else: This is exactly the incomplete deletion from the hook — 'done' after touching only the primary row leaves the same content recoverable from at least three other places.

contentSections.synthesis: A genuine deletion has to reach every place the content actually lives — primary record, vector index, any derived summaries that absorbed it, and a defined answer for backups — not just the first table a query happens to touch. This is real engineering work that has to be designed in from the start (which stores need a delete-cascade, what the backup retention policy commits to), not something added as an afterthought once someone asks.

contentSections.body: Regulatory frameworks like GDPR and CCPA give this a name ("right to erasure" / "right to delete") and real teeth in jurisdictions where they apply, but the engineering obligation is the same regardless of which specific law covers a given user: a deletion request that only removes the record you happen to think of first isn't a deletion, it's an illusion of one. Worth designing for from the moment a memory system is built — a cascading delete function that's exercised and tested, not written for the first time under pressure the day a real request arrives.

A genuine deletion request has to reach every store holding the content — primary record, vector index, derived summaries, and a defined backup policy — designed in from the start, not improvised the first time someone actually asks.

title: Decide what to store for seven agents
description: Seven drills applying this module's full toolkit — durability, deliberate writing, scoped and recency-aware retrieval, contradiction handling, and privacy — to new memory scenarios.

learningObjectives.text: Apply durability, write-trigger, retrieval-scoping, contradiction, and privacy judgment to new agent-memory scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — this is the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against memory scenarios you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: before writing to long-term memory, ask whether it's durable, whether the trigger caught the right thing, whether retrieval will scope and rank it correctly, whether it contradicts something already stored, and who else's privacy it touches.

title: Add memory with an explicit forgetting policy
description: Build a long-term memory layer with a deliberate write path, scoped and recency-aware retrieval, contradiction resolution, and a working expiry policy — applying every principle from this module to a real, working system.

learningObjectives.text: Design and build a memory layer with write rules, retrieval rules, and a working expiry policy

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Everything in this module was building toward one working thing: a memory layer that writes deliberately, retrieves what's actually relevant now, resolves contradiction instead of accumulating it, and genuinely forgets what should expire — not a system that stores everything and hopes similarity search sorts it out later.

contentSections.title: A memory layer with an explicit forgetting policy
contentSections.brief: Build a memory layer for an agent of your choice (reuse one from an earlier module, or a small new one) that: writes memory only through a deliberate trigger, not automatic logging; retrieves with both scope filtering and a similarity-plus-recency score; detects and resolves at least one genuine contradiction; and implements a working expiry mechanism for at least one time-bound memory category.
contentSections.deliverable: The write, retrieval, contradiction-resolution, and expiry code; a log showing at least 5 real writes with the trigger's reasoning for each (why it did or didn't store something); a demonstrated contradiction being resolved (old memory superseded, not just duplicated); and a demonstrated expiry actually removing or hiding a time-bound memory after its window passes.

stages.title: Build the deliberate write path
stages.instructions: Implement a write trigger that decides, per turn, whether something durable was said — per lesson two, checking against the actual durability test (preference, correction, or decision), not a loose proxy. Run it against at least 10 varied test messages (some that should store, some that shouldn't) and confirm the boundary lands correctly.

stages.title: Build scoped, recency-aware retrieval
stages.instructions: Implement retrieval that filters by scope (user, and project or category if relevant to your agent) before ranking, and blends similarity with a recency factor per lesson three. Test it against a case with two topically similar but differently-aged memories and confirm the more recent one ranks appropriately higher when it should.
stages.checkpoint: A retrieval function demonstrated to correctly prefer a more recent memory over a stale, similarly-worded one on at least one test case.

stages.title: Detect and resolve one real contradiction
stages.instructions: Write two memories for the same subject where the second genuinely contradicts the first (like the team-change example from this module). Implement the check-and-supersede logic from lesson four and confirm the old memory is marked supersededBy and excluded from normal retrieval, while still present in storage.

stages.title: Implement and demonstrate expiry
stages.instructions: Pick a time-bound memory category relevant to your agent, write one with an explicit expiresAt, and implement the check that excludes or removes it from retrieval once expired. Demonstrate it working — retrievable before the expiry point, not retrievable after.

rubric.criterion: Writes are deliberate, not automatic
rubric.meets: A real trigger decides per-turn whether to write, tested against both messages that should and shouldn't store, with visible reasoning for each call.

rubric.criterion: Retrieval is scoped before it's ranked
rubric.meets: A scope filter (user, and project/category if relevant) narrows the candidate pool before similarity-and-recency scoring runs.

rubric.criterion: Recency genuinely affects ranking
rubric.meets: A demonstrated case shows a more recent memory outranking a stale, topically similar one, not just similarity alone.

rubric.criterion: Contradiction is detected and resolved, not just stored twice
rubric.meets: A genuine contradiction results in the old memory marked superseded and excluded from normal retrieval, with an audit trail preserved.

rubric.criterion: Expiry actually works

rubric.criterion: The write log is honest and specific

contentSections.body: A memory layer earns its name from what this lab demonstrated working, not described: deliberate writes, scoped and recency-aware retrieval, real contradiction resolution, and expiry that actually removes what should no longer be there.
