learningObjectives.text: Apply claim-traceability, citation, gap-flagging, conflict-disclosure, and verification judgment to new agent-output scenarios

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — this is the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against citation and grounding scenarios you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: before trusting a cited answer, ask whether each claim actually points somewhere real and locatable, whether an honest gap got flagged instead of filled, whether a conflict got disclosed instead of hidden, and whether anything actually checked that the cited text supports the claim.

title: Add citation checking to your agent
description: Build a real citation-extraction and grounding-verification pipeline for a retrieval-based agent, then seed deliberate fabrications and prove the checker catches them.

learningObjectives.text: Build and validate an automated citation-verification checker against seeded fabrications

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Everything in this module was building toward one working thing: a checker that catches an unsupported claim before a person does — tested against fabrications you plant on purpose, not trusted because the code looks reasonable.

contentSections.title: A citation checker for a retrieval-based agent
contentSections.brief: Take a retrieval-based agent of your choice (reuse one from an earlier module, or a small new Q&A agent over a document set you have on hand) and add: structured citation generation that references only real, retrieved chunks; an automated verifier that checks each claim against its cited source text; and a test pass where you deliberately plant fabricated or unsupported claims into a set of outputs and confirm the verifier catches them.
contentSections.deliverable: The citation-generation and verification code; a set of at least 8 claim-citation pairs run through the verifier, at least 3 of them deliberately fabricated or unsupported (a false claim, a real citation that doesn't actually say the claim, a claim extended past what the source covers) and at least 5 genuinely well-supported; and a report showing the verifier's calls against all of them, including any false positives or false negatives it produced.

stages.title: Build structured, real citation generation
stages.instructions: Per lesson two, constrain the agent's citations to reference only chunk ids from documents actually retrieved this run, with a stable chunk identifier and the supporting quote. Confirm with at least 3 real questions that every citation produced points at a chunk that genuinely exists in what was retrieved.
stages.checkpoint: At least 3 outputs with citations, each citation verified by hand to reference a real, retrieved chunk with a correct chunk id.

stages.title: Build the grounding verifier
stages.instructions: Per lesson five, implement verifyGrounding: for each claim-citation pair, check whether the cited chunk's text actually supports the claim, with an explicit definition of "support" in the verifier's instructions. Run it against the well-supported outputs from stage one and confirm it correctly marks them supported.
stages.checkpoint: The verifier run against known-good claim-citation pairs, correctly marking all of them supported.

stages.title: Plant fabrications and test detection
stages.instructions: Deliberately construct at least 3 unsupported cases: a claim with no basis in any retrieved source, a claim citing a real chunk that doesn't actually say it, and a claim that extends a real cited fact past what the source covers (per lesson three's partial-coverage problem). Run all of them through the verifier and report exactly which it caught, which it missed, and any well-supported claim it incorrectly flagged.
stages.checkpoint: A report listing each planted fabrication, whether the verifier caught it, and the verifier's stated reason for each call — plus confirmation of zero or documented false positives on the known-good set.

rubric.criterion: Citations are real and locatable
rubric.meets: Every citation produced references an actual chunk from documents retrieved that run, with a stable identifier, not a free-text reference the model could fabricate.

rubric.criterion: The verifier checks support, not just presence
rubric.meets: The verifier evaluates whether the cited text actually contains or implies the claim, using an explicit stated definition of "support," not just whether a citation exists.

rubric.criterion: Fabrications were genuinely planted, not hypothetical
rubric.meets: At least 3 real, deliberately constructed unsupported or fabricated claims were run through the pipeline and reported on individually.

rubric.criterion: Detection results are reported honestly
rubric.meets: The report states plainly which planted fabrications the verifier caught and which it missed, rather than only reporting the successes.

rubric.criterion: False positives on good claims are checked too
rubric.meets: The known-good claim set was run through the verifier and any incorrect "unsupported" flags on genuinely supported claims are reported, not just accuracy on the fabricated set.

rubric.criterion: The pipeline is demonstrated working end to end
rubric.meets: A full run — generate citations, verify grounding, report results — is shown against real output, not described as a planned design.

contentSections.body: A citation checker earns its name from what this lab demonstrated it catching, on fabrications planted on purpose — not from code that looks like it should work and has never been tested against a real attempt to fool it.

title: Checkpoint — Grounding and Citation
description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from State and Durability (the previous module in the track), 2 from further back in Retrieval.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's grounding and citation vocabulary and reconnect it to the durability module that precedes it

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Grounding and Citation
contentSections.framing: No grade, no timer. Answer from memory before scrolling back.

questions.prompt: What's the test for whether a specific claim in an agent's output is grounded?

options.label: Whether it points to a specific, checkable place in a source that actually says it — confident phrasing doesn't substitute for this
Whether it's phrased with confident, authoritative-sounding language
Whether the overall answer, taken as a whole, sounds plausible

questions.explanation: Lesson one's core test — the reason a confident, uncited claim is functionally the same as a fabricated one to a reader who can't check it.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a well-formed, real citation on a claim guarantee the claim is actually grounded?

options.label: A real citation proves the source was actually retrieved and exists; it doesn't prove the cited text actually supports the specific claim next to it, which needs a separate check
It does guarantee it — a real citation is sufficient proof of grounding
Citations can never be verified automatically, only by a human reading the source

questions.explanation: Lesson five's core distinction — the reason an automated grounding verifier is a separate, necessary layer beyond citation-generation alone.

questions.prompt: What should an agent do when retrieved sources don't address part of a question?

options.label: Explicitly say so, rather than filling the gap with confident general knowledge that isn't actually stated anywhere in the retrieved sources
Answer using its own general knowledge, since a confident answer is more useful than an incomplete one
Refuse to answer any part of the question at all

questions.explanation: Lesson three's core pattern — explicit, structural permission to name a gap rather than fill it.

questions.prompt: When two retrieved sources genuinely conflict, what does an honest response require?

options.label: Surfacing that a conflict exists, even if a reasoned preference (like recency) is also stated
Silently preferring whichever source ranked highest in the similarity search
Averaging the two conflicting values together

questions.explanation: Lesson four's disclosure rule — a reasoned preference is fine, but it doesn't replace disclosing the conflict underneath it.

questions.prompt: What's the test for whether a piece of state must be durably checkpointed rather than left to be lost?

options.label: Whether losing it would force redoing real work — an API call, a scan, a write with an actual cost — to reconstruct it
Whether it's technically possible to store, regardless of what it costs to lose
Whether the run has been going for more than a few minutes

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here: this module's citation-verification lab applies the same discipline — don't trust a mechanism just because it looks like it should work, demonstrate it against a real test.

questions.prompt: Why does a resume path that always restarts from step 0, even with a correct checkpoint saved, produce redone work?

options.label: Writing a checkpoint and reading it on resume are separate pieces of code — a system can implement the write correctly and simply never call the read
Checkpoints saved to a database are unreliable and shouldn't be trusted on resume
Restarting from step 0 is actually the correct behavior in every case

questions.explanation: The presence-of-a-mechanism-isn't-use-of-a-mechanism pattern — the same gap this module names between a citation existing and a citation actually being checked.

questions.prompt: What makes a retried side effect provably safe, rather than merely probably fine?

options.label: An idempotency key the downstream system honors, or a locally-owned dedupe table checked before re-executing — something that positively recognizes a repeat
Catching any error the retry produces and treating it as evidence the step already succeeded
Trusting that most APIs happen to be idempotent by default

questions.explanation: The provably-safe-not-probably-fine standard — the same bar this module holds an automated grounding verifier to, tested against known cases rather than trusted on appearance.

questions.prompt: What should a multi-day resume check before continuing, per that module's lesson five?

options.label: Whether credentials, tool contracts, and the original wait's precondition are still valid — without redoing already-committed work
Nothing — a saved checkpoint is proof enough that everything is still fine
Every previously completed step, to be safe

questions.explanation: The targeted-revalidation-not-blind-trust pattern — the same shape as this module's insistence on verifying grounding automatically rather than trusting a citation's mere presence.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a correct final chatbot answer prove retrieval is working?

options.label: The model's own general knowledge can produce a correct answer even when retrieval returned nothing relevant, masking a retrieval failure
It does prove retrieval works — a correct answer is sufficient evidence
Final answers are never correct when retrieval fails

questions.explanation: Worth reconnecting here: this module's lesson three names the same failure mode directly — a model's general knowledge filling a genuine retrieval gap, dressed with the same confidence as a grounded answer.

questions.prompt: Where does semantic search tend to underperform, compared to keyword search?

options.label: Exact identifiers and rare precise strings — codes, IDs, exact names — where an embedding smooths a unique string into its general topic
Paraphrased queries that share no vocabulary with the target content
Nowhere — semantic search dominates keyword search in every case

questions.explanation: The no-single-signal-is-complete point — the same reasoning behind this module's rule that similarity rank alone can't resolve which of two conflicting sources is more likely correct.

contentSections.body: If these mostly landed, the grounding, citation, and verification vocabulary is solid enough to carry into the next phase's real-world agent builds — every one of which will need claims a person can actually check.
